families.title: Design FIR lowpass taps that fit a magnitude mask
description: The model gets a sampling rate, passband and stopband edges, a passband ripple limit, a stopband attenuation requirement and a maximum number of taps, and answers with the taps. The grader evaluates the magnitude response on a dense grid over both bands.

Difficulty rule: the tap limit is Kaiser's length estimate for the tighter of the two ripple requirements, times TAP_SLACK. With TAP_SLACK = 1.1 a Kaiser window design with some engineering margin (beta for a few dB more than required, cutoff placed inside the transition band) fits every instance, a Kaiser design at exactly the required attenuation fits about two thirds of them, and an equiripple design fits all of them with room to spare.
families.example_prompt:
Design a digital FIR lowpass filter that meets the specification below.

Sampling rate: 48000 Hz
Passband: 0 to 7300 Hz. The magnitude response must stay within 0.5 dB of 0 dB (between -0.5 dB and +0.5 dB).
Stopband: 12300 to 24000 Hz. The magnitude response must not exceed -60 dB.
Number of taps: at most 40.

The transition band between 7300 Hz and 12300 Hz is unconstrained. Linear phase is not required. Coefficients must be real numbers and are used exactly as written, in double precision. The magnitude response is checked on a dense frequency grid covering both bands, including the band edges.

Give the impulse response h[0], h[1], ..., h[N-1] as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"taps": [h0, h1, ...]}
```

families.title: A fixed-point biquad lowpass with exact integer semantics
description: The model gets a target (RBJ cookbook lowpass: f0, Q, sampling rate), an input bound, and the exact integer arithmetic of a Direct Form I biquad with int16 coefficients, an int32 accumulator and a rounding right shift. It answers with the integer coefficients and the shift.

The grader checks three things: the magnitude response of the integer filter against the target, the DC gain, and overflow, by running the integer recurrence on test inputs that include the worst case for the output.

Difficulty rule: f0 is low (0.8 % to 8 % of the sampling rate), where a1 is below -1 and does not fit Q15, and where plain rounding of the coefficients can leave a DC gain error. The reference uses Q14 (shift 14), rounds, and corrects b1 so the integer DC gain is exactly 1.
families.example_prompt:
Implement a second-order lowpass filter in fixed point.

Target: the RBJ Audio EQ Cookbook lowpass with f0 = 1837 Hz and Q = 1.5, at a sampling rate of 48000 Hz.

Arithmetic (Direct Form I), executed exactly as written for every sample n:
  acc  = b0*x[n] + b1*x[n-1] + b2*x[n-2] - a1*y[n-1] - a2*y[n-2]
  y[n] = (acc + (1 << (shift - 1))) >> shift      (for shift = 0: y[n] = acc)
- x and y are int16. b0, b1, b2, a1, a2 are int16 integers (-32768 to 32767). shift is an integer from 0 to 15.
- acc is int32: every partial sum, accumulated left to right, must stay within the int32 range.
- >> is an arithmetic right shift (rounds toward minus infinity).
- y[n] must fit in int16 without saturation or wraparound.
- Inputs are bounded: |x[n]| <= 14592. Initial state is zero.

Requirements:
- the magnitude response of the integer filter, H(z) = (b0 + b1 z^-1 + b2 z^-2) / (2^shift + a1 z^-1 + a2 z^-2) (rounding ignored), must stay within 0.02 (absolute, linear scale) of the target magnitude at every frequency from 0 to 24000 Hz;
- the DC gain must be within 0.02 dB of 0 dB;
- no overflow for any input within the bound;
- the filter must be stable.

Give the integers as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"b0": ..., "b1": ..., "b2": ..., "a1": ..., "a2": ..., "shift": ...}
```

families.title: An exponential moving average on bit shifts, as written in firmware
description: acc += ((x << F) - acc) >> k;   y = (acc + R) >> F

The model picks the shift k for a cutoff frequency, the number of fractional bits F and whether the output is rounded, so that the steady-state error for a constant input stays within a limit and nothing overflows int32 for the given ADC resolution.

The classic mistake is F = 0: (x - acc) >> k is zero whenever 0 <= x - acc < 2^k, so the output can stop up to 2^k - 1 LSB short of a constant input (a dead band). Fractional bits fix it, but they eat into the int32 headroom.

Difficulty rule: the cutoff target is within 10 % of the cutoff of one shift k, with a 20 % tolerance, so exactly one k qualifies. The reference uses that k, rounds the output, and takes the smallest F that meets the error limit.
families.example_prompt:
Configure an exponential moving average filter that runs on a microcontroller.

Input: signed 24-bit ADC samples, x[n] from -8388608 to 8388607, at 50000 samples per second.
Filter, executed for every sample with a 32-bit signed accumulator acc (initially any value the filter can reach):
  acc  = acc + (((x[n] << F) - acc) >> k)
  y[n] = (acc + R) >> F,   where R = 1 << (F - 1) if the output is rounded and F > 0, otherwise R = 0
>> is an arithmetic right shift (rounds toward minus infinity). Every intermediate value (x[n] << F, the difference, acc, acc + R) must fit in int32.

Requirements:
- cutoff: the -3 dB frequency of the linearized filter H(z) = 2^-k / (1 - (1 - 2^-k) z^-1) must be within 20 % of 130 Hz;
- steady-state error: for every constant input value, once the output stops changing, |x - y| must be at most 1 LSB, from any starting state;
- no int32 overflow for any input sequence within the ADC range.

Give your choice as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"k": ..., "frac_bits": ..., "round_output": true}
```

families.title: A unity-gain Sallen-Key lowpass from standard values
description: The model picks R1 and R2 from the E24 series and C1 and C2 from E12 for a target natural frequency f0 and quality factor Q. ngspice runs an AC sweep of the circuit; the grader measures f0 where the phase crosses -90 degrees and Q as the gain there (for this circuit, |H(j w0)| = Q).

Difficulty rule: the reference is the best E24/E12 combination found by exhaustive search over the capacitor pairs; instances are kept only when it lands within half of each tolerance. The negative is the equal-component design (R1 = R2, C1 = C2), which always gives Q = 0.5.
families.example_prompt:
Design a unity-gain Sallen-Key lowpass filter from standard component values.

Circuit (ideal op-amp wired as a voltage follower):
  input -> R1 -> node A;  node A -> R2 -> node B;  C1 from node A to the output;  C2 from node B to ground;
  op-amp non-inverting input at node B, output fed back to its inverting input.

Target: natural frequency f0 = 7.9 kHz and quality factor Q = 1.
Measured by AC simulation: f0 is where the phase of Vout/Vin crosses -90 degrees, and Q is |Vout/Vin| at that frequency.

Requirements:
- f0 within 2 % of the target, Q within 3 % of the target;
- R1 and R2 from the E24 series, between 1 kΩ and 1 MΩ;
- C1 and C2 from the E12 series, between 100 pF and 1 µF.

Give the values in ohms and farads as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"r1": 10000, "r2": 22000, "c1": 2.2e-8, "c2": 4.7e-9}
```
(those numbers only show the format)

families.title: Reach a gain and a bandwidth with a finite-GBW op-amp
description: The model cascades up to three non-inverting stages built from a single-pole op-amp model and E96 resistors. ngspice runs an AC sweep; the grader measures the low-frequency gain and the -3 dB bandwidth.

Difficulty rule: the bandwidth requirement is 85 % of what n equal stages reach (n = 2 or 3) and more than 10 % above what n - 1 stages reach, so one textbook stage with the whole gain is never enough. The gain tolerance (1 %) also makes the finite open-loop gain matter at high stage gains.
families.example_prompt:
Design a voltage amplifier from non-inverting op-amp stages.

Op-amp model: single pole, open-loop DC gain 100000 (100 dB), gain-bandwidth product 10 MHz, otherwise ideal (infinite input impedance, zero output impedance, no offset, no slew-rate limit).
Each stage is a non-inverting amplifier: Rf from the output to the inverting input, Rg from the inverting input to ground, ideal gain 1 + Rf/Rg. Stages are cascaded directly, the first stage driven by the input.

Requirements, measured by AC simulation of the whole chain:
- gain at 1 Hz within 1 % of 1100 V/V;
- -3 dB bandwidth (where the gain falls to 1/sqrt(2) of its 1 Hz value) at least 160 kHz;
- 1 to 3 stages; every resistor from the E96 series, between 100 Ω and 1 MΩ.

Give the stages in order as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"stages": [{"rf": 10000, "rg": 1000}]}
```
(that example shows the format only)

families.title: A loaded divider that holds its window at every tolerance corner
description: The model picks R1 and R2 from a given series. The supply has a tolerance, the resistors have a tolerance, and the output drives a load (an ADC input, say) that has a tolerance of its own. ngspice runs an operating point at each of the sixteen corners (supply, R1, R2 and load each at either limit); every corner must land inside the output window, and the supply current must stay under a limit.

Difficulty rule: the window is 1.3 times the smallest worst-case spread any pair in the series can reach under the current limit, rounded up. The current limit keeps the divider's total resistance comparable to the load, and the load's own spread keeps R2 from simply being made large, so the two pull against each other. A design that ignores the load misses the window.
families.example_prompt:
Design a resistive divider that holds its output window over all tolerances.

Circuit: supply -> R1 -> output; R2 from the output to ground; a load of 47 kΩ ± 20 % from the output to ground.
Supply: 24 V ± 5 %. Resistors: E96 series, ± 1 %, between 100 Ω and 10 MΩ.

Requirements, checked by simulation at all sixteen corners (supply, R1, R2 and load each at either tolerance limit):
- output voltage between 6.5 V and 9.5 V at every corner;
- current drawn from the supply at most 330 µA at every corner.

Give R1 and R2 in ohms as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"r1": ..., "r2": ...}
```

families.title: Tune a PID for overshoot, settling time and control effort
description: The plant is a stable third-order lag. The model answers with parallel PID gains; the derivative filter time constant is fixed by the spec. The grader closes the loop and simulates a unit reference step.

Difficulty rule: a reference PID is built by textbook pole cancellation (series form, Ti = tau1, Td = tau2) with its gain set by bisection for half the allowed overshoot. The settling-time limit is the reference's settling time times 1.25 and the control-effort limit its peak control signal times 1.5, both rounded up to two significant digits.
families.example_prompt:
Tune a PID controller for the plant below.

Plant: G(s) = 4.3 / ((9.7 s + 1)(2.6 s + 1)(0.34 s + 1))   (time in seconds)
Controller: C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd*s/(Tf*s + 1), with Tf = 0.068 s fixed.
Loop: unity negative feedback, e = r - y, u = C(s) e, y = G(s) u.

For a unit step in the reference r at t = 0, with zero initial conditions, simulated from 0 to 12 s:
- overshoot of y at most 15 % (overshoot = (max y - 1) * 100 %),
- settling time at most 3.7 s (the time after which |y - 1| stays within 2 %),
- peak control signal |u(t)| at most 200 (including the jump at t = 0),
- steady-state error |1 - y(inf)| at most 0.5 %,
- the closed loop must be stable.

Give the gains as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"kp": ..., "ki": ..., "kd": ...}
```

families.title: Design a lead/lag compensator for phase margin, gain margin and bandwidth
description: The plant is an integrator with two lags. The model answers with a first-order compensator C(s) = K (s/z + 1)/(s/p + 1). The grader computes the margins of L = C G and checks closed-loop stability.

Difficulty rule: the minimum crossover frequency is set so that, at 1.2 times that frequency, the plant needs between 20 and 50 degrees of phase lead on top of the required phase margin plus 5 degrees. A textbook single-lead design (maximum phase lead placed at the crossover) then meets every requirement; a pure gain does not.
families.example_prompt:
Design a compensator for the plant below.

Plant: G(s) = 17 / (s (1.9 s + 1)(0.37 s + 1))   (time in seconds)
Compensator: C(s) = K (s/z + 1) / (s/p + 1), with z > 0 and p > 0 in rad/s.
Loop: unity negative feedback, loop transfer function L(s) = C(s) G(s).

Requirements on L:
- phase margin at least 45 degrees,
- gain margin at least 8 dB,
- gain crossover frequency (where |L(jw)| = 1) at least 0.65 rad/s,
- the closed loop must be stable.

Give K, z and p as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"k": ..., "z": ..., "p": ...}
```

families.title: Discretize a continuous PID at a given sample time
description: The model gets a plant, a continuous PID with a filtered derivative and a sample time, and answers with the coefficients of the discrete controller. The grader closes the loop around the plant sampled with a zero-order hold and compares the sampled step response with the continuous loop's response.

Difficulty rule: the tolerance is 1.25 times the worst error of three standard discretizations (Tustin, backward Euler, forward Euler for the integral with backward Euler for the derivative), rounded up to two significant digits, and at least 0.01. Any of those methods passes; forgetting the sample time in the integral term does not.
families.example_prompt:
Discretize the continuous PID controller below for a digital implementation.

Plant: G(s) = 4.3 / ((4.3 s + 1)(0.97 s + 1))   (time in seconds)
Continuous controller: C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd*s/(Tf*s + 1), with
  Kp = 3.29, Ki = 0.624, Kd = 2.6, Tf = 0.19 s.
Sample time: Ts = 0.077 s.

The discrete controller runs once per sample as
  u[k] = -a1*u[k-1] - a2*u[k-2] + b0*e[k] + b1*e[k-1] + b2*e[k-2],
that is C(z) = (b0 + b1 z^-1 + b2 z^-2) / (1 + a1 z^-1 + a2 z^-2), with e[k] = r[k] - y[k].
The plant is driven through a zero-order hold and y is sampled at the same instants.

Requirement: for a unit step in r at t = 0, the sampled closed-loop output y[k] must stay within 0.11 of the continuous closed loop's step response at t = k*Ts, for every sample from 0 to 6.2 s, and the discrete closed loop must be stable. Use 0 for coefficients you do not need.

Give the coefficients as a JSON object at the end of your answer, in a ```json code block:

```json
{"b": [b0, b1, b2], "a": [a1, a2]}
```
